title: goto
alt: Neal Stephenson thinks it's cute to name his labels 'dengo'
transcript:
[Sideways view of Cueball sitting at computer, thinking.]
Cueball: I could restructure the program's flow
Cueball: or use one little 'GOTO' instead.

[Cueball starts typing.]
Cueball: Eh, screw good practice. How bad can it be?
Text on computer: goto main_sub3;
*Compile*

[We now have a view from behind Cueball. Cueball looks at the computer.]

[A raptor jumps into the panel, pushing Cueball off his chair.]
explanation:
A  statement is a construct found in many computer languages that causes control flow to go from one place in a program to another, without returning, such destination can be identified with a label. Once common in computer programming, its popularity diminished in the 1960s and 1970s as focus on  became the norm. 's article "Go To Statement Considered Harmful" in particular contributed to the decline of goto.

Often, people learning programming are told that goto statements are bad and should be avoided, but Cueball sees no harm in using one goto to avoid rewriting much of his program, most likely written in the . As a result, he is attacked by a velociraptor. The joke is an exaggeration of how harmful goto statements are, or what people make them out to be, implying the reason of its overwhelming avoidance, which is to "instead focus on good code style", can be indistinguishable to "because they cause velociraptor attacks". Velociraptor attacks are a running joke (and fear) often expressed in xkcd. 

The statement goto main_sub3; means that it should go to the third main  when executed. This shows poor , as its unclear what the usage of the subroutine is. Jokingly, this is a hard thing to get right in computer science. The line also suggests that there are two other subroutines marked by similar labels. If this is written in C, this would contradict Cueball's implication that this is his first incident, as labels are only used when called by goto statements.

The title text refers to , an author of cyberpunk novels. The joke is that one of Stephenson's characters in  is named Goto Dengo, which can be represented as goto dengo;, which follows correct C grammar and is charming to the eyes of Stephenson.
